prompt: Let $n$ be a positive integer. Find, with proof, the smallest integer $k$ for which every subset of $\{1,2,\dots,2024n\}$ of size $k$ contains two elements $a,b$ such that $\gcd(a,b)\le2023$.

solutions.title: Differences and the multiples of 2024
solutions.body:
**Claim: $k=n+1$.**

*$k>n$:* the set $\{2024,2\cdot2024,\dots,n\cdot2024\}$ has $n$ elements and any two of its elements have gcd a multiple of $2024$, so $\gcd\ge2024$. Hence a subset of size $n$ need not contain a pair with $\gcd\le2023$.

*$k=n+1$ works:* take any $n+1$ elements $a_1<a_2<\dots<a_{n+1}$ of $\{1,\dots,2024n\}$ and suppose every pair has $\gcd\ge2024$. For $i<j$, $\gcd(a_i,a_j)$ divides $a_j-a_i>0$, so $a_j-a_i\ge\gcd(a_i,a_j)\ge2024$. Therefore consecutive elements differ by at least $2024$ and
$$a_{n+1}\ge a_1+2024n\ge1+2024n>2024n,$$
a contradiction. So some pair has $\gcd\le2023$. ∎

prompt: Given $x,y,z\ge0$ and $x\sqrt{yz}+y\sqrt{xz}+z\sqrt{xy}\ge12$, find, with proof, the minimum possible value of $x+y+z$.

solutions.title: Substitute squares and use $(ab+bc+ca)^2\ge3abc(a+b+c)$
solutions.body:
Write $x=a^2,\ y=b^2,\ z=c^2$ with $a,b,c\ge0$. Then $x\sqrt{yz}=a^2bc$ and the condition reads $abc(a+b+c)\ge12$.

For real numbers, $(ab+bc+ca)^2\ge3abc(a+b+c)$ (it is $\frac12\sum(ab-bc)^2\ge0$). Hence $(ab+bc+ca)^2\ge36$, so $ab+bc+ca\ge6$, and
$$x+y+z=a^2+b^2+c^2\ge ab+bc+ca\ge6 .$$
Equality: $x=y=z=2$ gives $3\cdot2\sqrt4=12$ and $x+y+z=6$. The minimum is $6$. ∎

prompt: Moby has an infinite piece of paper, an infinite straightedge, and a magic triangle. The paper starts with two points a distance $1$ away. With the straightedge, he can connect any two points to form a line. With the magic triangle, he can take two points $A$ and $B$ and draw the two points $C$ and $D$ such that $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle ABD$ are equilateral triangles. He can also draw a point at the intersection of any two lines or line segments. With finitely many operations, can Moby draw a square on the paper? A proof in the affirmative should consist of a clear depiction or description of steps taken.
answer: No: every constructible point has coordinates in $\mathbb Q\times\sqrt3\,\mathbb Q$, which contains no square.

solutions.title: An invariant: points of the form $(p,q\sqrt3)$
solutions.body:
**Answer: no.** Place the starting points at $A_0=(0,0)$ and $B_0=(1,0)$ and call a point *good* if it has the form $(p,\,q\sqrt3)$ with $p,q\in\mathbb Q$. We show every point Moby can ever draw is good.

- The starting points are good.
- *Intersections.* Write good points as $(p,\eta)$ with $\eta=y/\sqrt3\in\mathbb Q$, i.e. use the coordinates $(x,\eta)$. In these coordinates a line through two good points is a line with rational equation $ux+v\eta=w$ ($u,v,w\in\mathbb Q$), and the intersection of two non-parallel such lines is a point with rational $(x,\eta)$: good.
- *Magic triangle.* If $A$, $B$ are good, $B-A=(\Delta x,\ \Delta\eta\sqrt3)$, then $C,D=A+R_{\pm60^\circ}(B-A)$ where
$$R_{60^\circ}(\Delta x,\Delta\eta\sqrt3)=\Big(\tfrac{\Delta x}2-\tfrac{3\Delta\eta}2,\ \sqrt3\big(\tfrac{\Delta x}2+\tfrac{\Delta\eta}2\big)\Big),$$
which is a good vector. So $C,D$ are good.

Now suppose a square with consecutive vertices $P_0,P_1,P_2,P_3$ had been drawn (its vertices are drawn points, or intersections of drawn lines and hence also good). Let $P_1-P_0=(p,q\sqrt3)$ with $p,q\in\mathbb Q$. Rotating by $90^\circ$ gives $P_3-P_0=(\mp q\sqrt3,\ \pm p)$. This is a difference of good points, so its first coordinate $\mp q\sqrt3$ must be rational: $q=0$; and its second coordinate $\pm p$ must lie in $\sqrt3\,\mathbb Q$: $p=0$. Then $P_1=P_0$, which is not a square. (Even if only the four side lines of the square are drawn, the same conclusion holds: in the coordinates $(x,\eta)$ a drawn line $ux+v\eta=w$ has normal $(u,v/\sqrt3)$ in the plane, and a perpendicular drawn line $u'x+v'\eta=w'$ must have $uu'+vv'/3=0$, so its normal has length exactly $\sqrt3$ times as large (take $(u',v')\propto(-v,3u)$). The spacings between the two pairs of parallel sides are $|\Delta w|/|n|$ and $|\Delta w'|/(\sqrt3|n|)$ with $\Delta w,\Delta w'$ rational, so they can never be equal and nonzero.)

Hence it is impossible for Moby to draw a square. ∎
